outcomes: Explain the development of modern evolutionary theory.
Apply classical and modern genetic approaches to the study of taxonomy and evolution.
Analyze non-human primate and hominin behavior, social organization, and morphology.
Integrate biological, geological, and archaeological evidence within the framework of the scientific method, in order to formulate interpretations of human evolution.
Integrate biological and social perspectives in the description and explanation of human diversity, with particular emphasis on the social impacts of those explanations.
Apply current examples of the interactions between culture and biology, particularly in the area of genetics and viruses, including zoonoses.
objectives: Define the discipline of anthropology and discuss the role of biological anthropology within the science, and understand its contributions to understanding humanity.

Understand genetic inheritance on an individual level, and a population level.
Assess current debates in human biological evidence and diversity.
Demonstrate an understanding of the classification, morphology , behavior and sustainability of the living primates.
Explain the various dating techniques and how they are used in paleoanthropology.
Explain how humans have changed and adapted, both physically and culturally, to their habitat through the process of evolution.
Understand the impact the Anthropocene has had on the global climate and the implications of that impact on the future of the species.

Identify and distinguish between the five basic types of construction. These would include Type I (concrete and steel), Type II (basic steel building), Type III (exterior wall noncombustible material with interior components either combustible or noncombustible), Type IV (heavy timber), and Type V (wood framed construction).

This would include the basic vertical fire resistive assemblies including Fire Wall, Fire Barrier, Fire Partition, Smoke Barrier, and Smoke Partition construction as noted in section 706, 707, 708, 709, and 710 of the International Building Code.

Examine, describe, and distinguish between the basic components active fire suppression systems and their proper applications in building and structures. These would include fire sprinklers (water), fire extinguishing systems (Halon, Ansul, Carbon Dioxide), Fire alarms, Stand pipe, and portable fire extinguishers.

Describe and apply the proper Means of Egress requirements for the Occupancies, Occupant Load, Type of Construction, and Location on property regulations. outcomes: Write text-based paragraphs (100-300 words or more) that summarize or respond to low-intermediate readings (Lexile Measure 740-1010), use a variety of rhetorical strategies, integrate newly-acquired low-intermediate academic vocabulary, include an effective topic sentence and support, and demonstrate general competency in the conventions of standard American English, containing some disruptive errors but allowing for understanding of meaning.

Communicate arguments and opinions at an increasing level of fluency which indicate a growing awareness of patterns and expectations of United States culture, especially in the college and work environments, by successfully responding to appropriate readings.
objectives: Evaluate and select evidence from fiction and non-fiction texts at a low-intermediate level (Lexile Measure 740-1010).
Create well-developed support for opinions through the writing process.
Write academic paragraphs which show control of morphology and frequently used syntactic structures (e.g. common word order, patterns, coordination, and subordination) at a low-intermediate level.
Create well-developed academic paragraphs with a variety of rhetorical strategies used in the United States.
Use the drafting and editing process to correct language at a low-intermediate level and avoid grammar, usage, and punctuation errors that interfere with meaning.
Recognize elements of an essay and how paragraphs relate to one another within an essay.
Demonstrate cultural awareness to communicate on matters encountered in work or school.

Recognize meanings of words based on their function in the sentence (parts of speech).
Practice skills necessary for success in higher education and be aware of cultural themes in readings about American culture.

rows.title: Introduction to Ethnic Studies
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, anti-blackness, self- determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, exploitation colonialism, xenophobia, intersectionality, and anti-racism as analyzed and studied in any one or more of the following: Native American Studies, African American Studies, Asian American Studies, and Latina and Latino American Studies.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino American communities to describe critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived experiences, and struggles of those groups with a particular emphasis on subjection or subject formation, agency, and group affirmation.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age, in Native American, African American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino American Communities.

Critically situate in historical context and review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and, enacted by Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans, enacted by Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans and/or Latina and Latino Americans are relevant to current and structural issues at the local, national, international, and transnational levels. Such issues may be communal, national, international, and transnational politics, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial thought, issues, and the practices and movements in Native American, Asian American, and/or Latina and Latino communities and a just and equitable society.
objectives: Define and distinguish foundational concepts of race, ethnicity, and racialization across Ethnic Studies.
Identify and critique manifestations of ethnocentrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, and anti-Blackness.
Analyze the structures and consequences of imperialism, settler colonialism, and exploitation colonialism.
Evaluate how equity, sovereignty, and self-determination are mobilized to resist oppression.
Apply theories of decolonization and liberation to case studies in U.S. and global contexts.
Examine intersections of race/racism with xenophobia, class, gender, sexuality, and ability.
Articulate anti-racist strategies and practices using Ethnic Studies frameworks in oral and written work.
Summarize key epistemologies and intellectual traditions from African American, Native American, Asian American, and Chicana/o/x/Latina/o/x Studies.
Identify the major historical events that have shaped the identity formation in communities of color.
Analyze the impact of generational trauma on communities through scholarly and cultural texts.
Examine cultural productions (literature, art, film, music) as sources of theory and knowledge.
Compare how different communities have articulated strategies of agency and group affirmation.
Apply Ethnic Studies knowledge to interpret contemporary issues facing marginalized groups.
Define the concept of intersectionality and explain its application in Ethnic Studies.
Examine how racism intersects with class, gender, sexuality, and ability in shaping lived experiences.
Analyze the role of sovereignty, tribal citizenship, and immigration status in racial identity.
Examine the intersection of religion, spirituality, and language with racial and ethnic identity formations.
Evaluate case studies of discrimination and resistance where multiple identity markers intersect.
Develop intersectional analyses of contemporary social issues using Ethnic Studies frameworks
Identify major social justice movements led by communities of color in U.S. history.
Analyze the strategies of solidarity and resistance used across different communities.
Evaluate the historical and contemporary significance of liberation struggles.
Examine how movements for justice intersect across race, gender, sexuality, class, and nation.
Connect historical struggles to contemporary political issues such as immigration, reparations, or multiculturalism.
Assess transnational connections in racial and ethnic justice movements.
Identify key anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial frameworks in Ethnic Studies.
Examine historical and contemporary abolitionist movements and their impacts.
Analyze case studies of anti-colonial and anti-imperial struggles in the U.S. and globally.
Critically evaluate strategies for building justice and equity across racial/ethnic communities.
Engage in classroom and community-based activities that practice anti-racist and decolonial methods.
Propose informed actions for contributing to justice, equity, and liberation beyond the classroom.

rows.title: Introduction to Chicanx and Latinx Studies
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Describe the cultural roots of the Chicanx and Latinx population.

Analyze and articulate concepts and theories from Chicanx and Latinx Studies and Ethnic Studies, including but not limited to critical race theory, intersectionality, voice of color thesis, interest convergence, differential racialization, majoritarian stories versus counter-stories, Latinidad, mestizaje, indigenismo, internal colonialism, cultural hegemony and denigration, language and colonized cultures, the imperial colonial dialectic, the concept of place and displacement, border theory, citizenship, transnationalism, historical materialism, Chicana and Latina feminisms, globalization, cultural studies, racial formation, and post-colonialism as they apply to the Chicanx and Latinx experience in the United States.
Assess educational, cultural, or political activism related to issues impacting the Chicanx and Latinx communities.

Identify and discuss examples of experiences of struggle, resistance, social justice, solidarity, and self-determination cross-culturally and transnationally that influence modern Chicanx and Latinx culture in the United States.
objectives: Describe the intersectional and interdisciplinary approaches to Chicanx and Latinx Studies.
Identify the range of issues, experiences, and methodologies that form the foundation of Chicanx and Latinx Studies.
Analyze the complex development of cultural identities of Chicanx and Latinx people and their influence on both the United States and the borderlands/frontera.
Define Latinidad and the inter- and intra-group relations of Chicanx and Latinx people.
Discuss the complicated constructions of "Chicanx" and "Latinx" identities and their relationship to race and ethnicity in the United States.
Identify theoretical frameworks in the field of Chicanx and Latinx studies.
Discuss the role of migration, immigration, and diaspora in the shaping of Chicanx and Latinx culture and identity.
Explain the intersectional relationships between Chicanx and Latinx communities of race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, class, religion, ability, and language.

rows.title: Native American History to 1871
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate active engagement with anti-racist issues, practices and movements to build a diverse, just and equitable society beyond the classroom as well as demonstrate the ability to think independently, review and analyze information reflectively, and reason logically based on review and interpretation of historical information.

Describe how struggle, resistance, social justice solidarity and liberation as experienced by Native Americans are relevant to current issues and reflect upon contemporary concerns of, and issues regarding, Native Americans in a global context and based on an understanding of US history.

Critically discuss the intersection of race and ethnicity with other forms of difference affected by hierarchy and oppression, such as class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability and/or age and be able to explain and interpret the laws created and implemented to enslave African people and the subsequent legacy of those laws on the status and identity of Native Americans and the implications of those laws for all of American society.

Apply theory to describe critical events in the histories, cultures, and intellectual traditions, with special focus on the lived-experiences and social struggles of Native Americans emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.

Analyze and articulate concepts of ethnic studies, including but not limited to race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, and anti-racism.
objectives: Examine the structures of Native American societies before the arrival of Europeans.
Convey the cause and impact of important events in American Indian studies.
Outline the scope and nature of North American Indian religions, describe the varieties of their religious experiences, and summarize key values associated with these experiences through 1871.
Describe the problem of "factionalism" through Native American History from about 1550 to 1871.

Compare and contrast the varieties of social organizations, economic systems, and political strategies existing in Native American societies at the time contact with Europeans, and how these changed through 1871.
Examine revitalization movements among Native Americans and describe the circumstances in which they occurred through 1871.
Analyze the development of the reservation system from its origins in the 1640s under Great Britain through the end of the Civil War.
Discuss the impact of westward movement on Native American societies focusing particularly on Indian-settler-army relationships.
Analyze the legal status of North American Indians under U.S. jurisdiction from 1776 to 1871.
Apply lessons of history to civic responsibilities.
Foster a better awareness of the American Indian in our community and an appreciation of their history and culture.
Develop a knowledge and appreciation of the contributions of Native American people to the American society.

rows.title: Asian American History
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate active engagement with anti-racist issues, practices and movements to build a diverse, just and equitable society by centering the experiences of Asian immigrants and their U.S.-born descendants in an effort to build a diverse, just and equitable society beyond the classroom.

Analyze and articulate how key concepts of ethnic studies, including but not limited to race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, colonization, decolonization and anti-racism, have shaped and continue to shape the experiences of Asian Americans in the United States.

Apply theory to describe the critical events in the histories, culture and intellectual traditions of Asian Americans, with special focus on the lived-experiences and social struggles of Asian immigrants and their U.S.-born descendants and the manners in which those experiences are affected by broader global historical processes.

Critically discuss the intersection of race and ethnicity with other forms of difference affected by hierarchy and oppression, such as class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability and/or age in the context of Asian American lives.

Describe how struggle, resistance, social justice, solidarity and liberation as experienced by Asian Americans are relevant to current issues by composing arguments based on the recognition, analysis, and interpretation of primary historical sources and secondary sources.
objectives: Convey the cause and impact of important events in historical eras in Asian American studies.
Critique primary and secondary historical sources; perspectives and debates in Asian American
studies.
Using varied scholarly sources, assess the importance of historical evidence from major eras,
political figures, legislative acts, social trends, and economic policy in Asian American studies.
Compare and contrast the experiences of marginalized groups with that of the dominant power
structure, including concerns of hierarchy, race, economic class, gender, sexuality, spirituality, national origins and immigration status in Asian American studies.
Examine the origins of anti-Asian racism in ideas such as Orientalism, the model minority stereotype, the “yellow peril,” and the idea of the perpetual foreigner.
Apply lessons of struggle, resistance, social justice, solidarity and liberation to politics, law, economics, and society in the United States.
Explore through the major historical eras, major discriminatory acts, and major contributions of
Asian Pacific Americans, and how these eras shaped the lived experiences and social struggles of Asian Americans.

Compare and contrast the experiences of Asians in America in the first period of open immigration (1848-1934), second period of closed immigration (1934-1965), and third period of preferential quota system (1965-present).

Identify and critique the roles of various Asian ethnicities in the development of various American, economic systems such as agribusiness, plantation economy, transportation, industries, business, information technology, and medical health fields.
Research and critique the reasons for the internment of Japanese Americans from 1941 through 1946.
Analyze U.S. relations with Asia from 19th century commercial investments to the era of the Cold War, decolonization and modern globalization.
Compare and contrast the roles of Asian Pacific American women in the development of their communities and families in different eras.
Examine the effects transnationalism, economic heterogeneity and inter-racialism have complicated stories of Asian American lives.
Critique U.S. immigration policies towards Asians and others from the 1800s to the present.
Examine ways that social movements and political organization have worked to include Asian Americans in a diverse, just and equitable society.
Compare and contrast Asian Pacific American history with the experiences of American Indians, Chicanos/Latinos, and African Americans.

Identify and explain the appropriate use of reference and thematic maps for different types of data to be displayed, e.g., road maps/Google Maps, nominal/categorical maps, isoline maps, choropleth, graduated symbol, proportional symbol, or dot density maps.

Interpret and analyze a variety of categorical and quantitative map symbols and extract data values from maps for specific locations, including but not limited to abstract reference map symbols, isolines (exact or estimated values, slope/rate of change), graduated symbol and dot density maps, etc.

Measure and analyze distance, area, location, and direction on maps or images, including one or more of the following: printed map scale, north arrow, map grid coordinates, or determining the map scale and location from ancillary information about features on the map.
objectives: Use critical thinking to identify and distinguish maps from other types of graphic images based on fundamental properties and elements of graphic design distinctive of maps.
Use critical thinking to evaluate the effect of subjective, alternative choices in map design, such as projections, scale, and symbols, on the accuracy, effectiveness, and usefulness of maps.
Demonstrate awareness of the wide variety of map types, map uses, and alternative forms of maps that may be used for similar purposes with varying levels of effectiveness.
Use standard methods and tools to make measurements, identify and interpret map features, and extract or derive data and information from printed or digital maps and images.

rows.title: Physical Geology Laboratory

rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Identify rock and mineral specimens, determine their composition through a variety of tests and describe how they are formed.

Analyze topographic maps and construct cross-sections to deduce the geologic features represented and determine what physiographic features are expressed in such diverse settings as deserts, glacially sculpted landscapes, river valleys and coastlines.
Identify geologic structures, faults and folds in 3-dimentional diagrams and be able to construct the same.

Recognize and analyze earthquake data. Determine the size and location of the event using the Richter Nomogram. Contour Mercalli Scale intensities and describe the likely effects of the event based on distance from the epicenter and the surface and subsurface geology.

Identify and describe plate tectonic conditions around the globe and illustrate specific locations where the three plate boundaries are exemplified.

Locate an earthquake, calculate its Richter magnitude and describe the intensity of the event according to the Modified Mercali scale.
Use field tests to identify both silicate and non-silicate minerals.
Identify mineral content and texture in igneous rocks in order to classify them and describe their process of formation.
Measure and describe grain size and or composition of sedimentary rocks in order to identify them and describe the environments in which they were created.
Characterize the texture and composition of metamorphic rocks in order to interpret their conditions of formation.
Use topographic maps to create cross-sections and identify the geologic structures they represent.
Create a geologic timeline with details showing major geologic events and evolutionary developments in life through time.
Analyze map and subsurface data to describe hydrologic systems, including river and groundwater systems.
Use surface expressions on maps to discern past glacial events and the structures left behind.
Analyze coastal maps and marine charts to describe coastal processes and geologic structures.

rows.title: African American History II
rows.title_printed: Course Outline: Riverside Community College District
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of the course, students should be able to demonstrate the following skills:
outcomes: Demonstrate active engagement with anti-racist issues, practices and movements to build a diverse, just and equitable society beyond the classroom as well as demonstrate the ability to think independently, review and analyze information reflectively, and reason logically based on review and interpretation of historical information.

Describe how struggle, resistance, social justice solidarity and liberation as experienced by African Americans are relevant to current issues and reflect upon contemporary concerns of, and issues regarding, African Americans in a global context and based on an understanding of US history.

Critically discuss the intersection of race and ethnicity with other forms of difference affected by hierarchy and oppression, such as class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability and/or age and be able to explain and interpret the laws created and implemented to enslave African people and the subsequent legacy of those laws on the status and identity of African Americans and the implications of those laws for all of American society.

Apply theory to describe critical events in the histories, cultures, and intellectual traditions, with special focus on the lived-experiences and social struggles of African Americans emphasizing agency and group-affirmation.

Analyze and articulate concepts of ethnic studies, including but not limited to race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, and anti-racism.
objectives: Identify the ways that freed African Americans dealt with economic and social change, including employment and education.
Describe the role of the Freedmen’s Bureau in the Reconstruction period.
Explain the role of the black church in the creation of community and political leaders.
Describe the reaction of white Americans to the end of the war, including violence and black codes.
Analyze how Congress and President Johnson influenced Reconstruction through the Reconstruction Acts.
Explain how the Thirteenth and Fourteenth amendments affected the African-American community.
Describe segregation and how the Plessy v. Ferguson decision contributed to it.
Explain the role that violence played in the lives of African Americans, including race riots and lynching.
Analyze the reasons behind the migration of African Americans to Africa, the western United States, and Southern
cities, and the effects of that migration.
Express how the justice system has historically been applied to African Americans.
Compare and contrast the two philosophies of African-American progress, represented by Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. DuBois.
Explain the role of African-American soldiers in the U.S. Armed Forces from the Civil War to World War I.
Describe the reasons behind the Great Migration.
Explain the roots of the Harlem Renaissance and the Jazz Age and identify a few of the major artists associated with it.
Describe the reasons behind the resurrection of the Ku Klux Klan and the changes in the organization during the 1920s.
Explain some of the causes of the Great Depression and why African Americans were heavily impacted.
Describe the steps the NAACP took during the 1930s to challenge racial inequality in schools.
Analyze how President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s First New Deal affected African Americans.
Explain how Brown vs. the Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas, changed the face of segregation.
Analyze the Little Rock desegregation challenge and how it reflected the white backlash to the progress of African Americans.
Describe a few of the grassroots efforts toward progress, including sit-ins, freedom rides, and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC).
Discuss how the legal changes in the 1960s offered more opportunities for African Americans.
Analyze how the black power and black nationalism grew out of the civil rights movement and the reasons behind urban violence during the late 1960s.
Trace the development of an increased political voice of African Americans from the local to the national level, including those who ran for president.
Identify how No Child Left Behind, the Welfare Reform Act, and affirmative action affects the lives of African Americans.
Analyze the ways in which African Americans have not yet reached economic equality with white Americans.
Explain how incarceration and police brutality continue to be an important issue in the African-American community and the nation at large.
Discuss the challenges and divisions exposed by the 2016 election, the Obama presidency, and the Trump era, along with the protests and reactions that occurred afterward.

objectives: At the novice level:

Perform and document an assessment of specific patient populations encompassing values, preferences, expressed needs, and the impact of developmental, emotional, cultural, religious, and spiritual influences on the patient’s health status.

Select patient-centered health teaching interventions that address such topics as healthy lifestyles, risk-reducing behaviors, developmental needs, activities of daily living, and preventative self-care.
Incorporate patient-centered care interventions that demonstrate sensitivity and respect for the diversity of the human experience.
Use evidence-based practices to guide clinical decision-making in the delivery of quality, safe nursing care.
Safely perform psychomotor nursing skills, as outlined in the Nursing Skills Across the Curriculum, within the context of the patient situation.
Demonstrate patient advocacy skills in the care of assigned patients and their families.
Ethical and Legal Principles
Incorporate professional standards, ethical behaviors, and legal principles of nursing practice.
Support the image of nursing by modeling the values and articulating the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of the nursing profession.

Demonstrate professional attitudes and behaviors, including attention to appearance, demeanor, respect for self and others, and attention to professional boundaries with patients and families as well as caregivers.

Leadership Principles
Implement organizational and time management skills to safely manage the health care needs of assigned patients.

Caring
Incorporate interventions to address patient and family needs that include input from other health care team members when planning or providing patient-centered care.
Implement nursing interventions appropriate to the patient’s developmental level; physical and psychological needs; spiritual beliefs; and culture.
Plan nursing care to facilitate the achievement of expected patient outcomes in a collaborative and caring manner that provides direction for continuity of care.
Incorporate relationship-centered care principles when caring for self and interacting with patients, families, peers, and other members of the health care team.
Collaborative Relationships
Incorporate effective communication techniques to foster positive professional working relationships.
Foster collaborative relationships with the health care team, using appropriate communication skills, to improve patient outcomes and ensure the delivery of evidence-based patient-centered care.
Select and perform interventions that promote quality, safe patient-centered care as a member of the health care team that contributes to improving patient care outcomes.
Summarize and document patient care data to inform the health care team and contribute to clinical decision-making.
Summarize and report relevant information to an appropriate health care team member to improve patient outcomes.
Critical Thinking
Demonstrate clinical reasoning and judgment skills in providing quality, safe patient-centered care to assigned patients.
Collect data, identify problems, establish goals, and select interventions based on the patient’s immediate or anticipated needs of the patient and situation.
Perform ongoing evaluation of expected outcomes and interventions for assigned patients and revise the individualized plan of care as needed.
Participate in self-reflection strategies to identify professional learning needs.
Incorporate quality improvement activities to identify and prevent potential problems that may interfere with the delivery of safe patient care in a variety of health care settings.
Nursing Informatics
Demonstrate computer literacy, including the ability to use desktop applications and mobile technology to promote effective communication and support decision-making.
Competently use patient care technologies, information systems, and mobile technology to support safe nursing care for assigned patients in a variety of health care settings.
Demonstrate the use of information technology systems to prevent the risk of errors and improve clinical outcomes in the delivery of safe patient care.
Access data and documents using the nursing process via electronic health record, abiding by all ethical and legal standards.
